By way of award dated 21.02.2012, being assailed through the present appeal, the learned Tribunal has awarded a sum of Rs.1,75,000/-, to respondent Jaiwanti, along-with .
interest @ 7.5% per annum, from the date of filing of the petition till the date of deposit of the amount.
While deciding the said claim petition, the ultimate liability to pay the amount of has been put on the owner and driver of vehicle No. HP09- 0735.
The Insurance-Company has been exonerated by the learned Tribunal.

rt 3. The parties to the present lis are hereinafter referred to, in the same manner, as were, referred to,
by the learned Tribunal.

4. Brief facts, leading to the filing of present appeal, before this Court, may be summed up as under:-
5. Petitioner Jaiwanti has filed the claim petition, under Section 166 of the M.V. Act, seeking compensation on account of death of her son Sanjay, in motor vehicle accident, against the owner,
driver and insurer of truck No. HP09-0735 (hereinafter referred to as the 'offending vehicle').
6.
During the pendency of the lis before the learned Tribunal, respondent No.1 (owner) had died and his legal heirs i.e. respondents No. 1(a) to 1(e), were impleaded in the claim petition.

7. The compensation has been sought on the ground .
that on 23.03.2004, Sanjay Kumar @ Sanju along-with Hem Raj, who was his neighbour, had hired the offending vehicle for loading their goods and after loading the goods, they were of travelling in the offending vehicle, as care taker of their goods.
They had also to unload the goods at the destination.
rt

Respondent No.2 was driving the offending vehicle, in a rash and negligent manner and when, the offending vehicle reached at the place, known as Surahi khud, at about 7.30 p.m., respondent No.2 lost control over it and vehicle rolled down in the 400 deep gorge.
Consequently, Sanjay Kumar and Hem Raj had expired on the spot.
8. Sanjay @ Sanju, at the time of his death, was about 21 years of age.

He was doing Carpenter work,
as well as, agricultural work and his income has been pleaded as Rs.7,000/- per month.

14.1. On merits, the contents of claim petition have been denied by pleading that FIR was registered against respondent No.2, but, same was registered on wrong facts.
He has also admitted that Sanjay Kumar @ Sanjay was a casual labourer.
The claim petition has further been contested, in which, he has feigned his ignorance about the fact whether the deceased were travelling in the vehicle, as per the case set up by the petitioner.
The cause of accident, according to respondent No.1, was latent mechanical defect.

15. Respondent No.2 has filed his separate reply, in which, he has also taken the plea that though,
accident in question had taken place, but, the same had not taken place .
due to his rash and negligent driving.
He has also termed the FIR registered against him, as having been lodged on the basis of wrong facts.
He has categorically denied that deceased of was travelling in the vehicle as a care taker of the goods.

16. The Insurance-Company has filed its separate reply rt by taking preliminary objections that vehicle in question was being plied in violation of the terms and conditions of the Insurance policy;
and that the deceased was travelling in the vehicle as a gratuitous passenger.
These facts have been pleaded with a view to get rid of the liability to pay the compensation.
Rest of the contents have been denied mainly, for want of knowledge.
17. Thus, the respondents have prayed for the dismissal of the claim petition.

Thereafter, the parties to the lis were directed to rt adduce evidence.

After the closure of evidence, upon hearing the learned counsel appearing for the parties, the learned Tribunal has awarded the compensation to the petitioner, however, the liability has been fastened upon the owner and driver of vehicle, by exonerating the Insurance- Company.

20. Feeling aggrieved from the said award, the present appeal has been filed by LRs of owner, before this Court assailing the award, mainly, on the ground that the impugned award is not sustainable in the eyes of law, as, the petitioner has miserably failed to prove the fact that the accident in question had taken place due to rash and negligent driving of respondent No.2.

The Tribunal, according to the appellants, has wrongly relied upon the statement of PW-3.
21.

Findings have further been assailed on the ground that the registration of FIR under Sections 279, 337, 304A IPC against the driver is not sufficient to conclude that respondent .
No.2 was driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner.

Similarly, statement of RW-3 Govind Ram has also been highlighted to probabilise the fact that Hem Raj and Sanjay Kumar had kept some articles at Pandoh which were to be taken to village Chapran.

24. The findings have further assailed on the ground that the learned Tribunal ought to have clubbed both the claim petitions for the purpose of recording evidence and failure to do so has occasioned in miscarriage of justice.

25. On the basis of above facts, Ms. Anu Tuli Azta, Advocate has argued that appeal may kindly be accepted and the impugned award may kindly be set aside, by .
dismissing the claim petition.

26. It has also been argued that in case, this Court comes to the conclusion that the petitioner is entitled for of compensation, then, the liability to pay the compensation should be saddled on the Insurance-Company as the vehicle rt in question was insured with respondent No.3 and no fundamental breach of insurance policy has been proved or probabilised by the Insurance-Company, in this case.

27. Per contra, Mr. B.M.Chauhan, learned Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr. Amit Himalvi, Advocate appearing for respondent No.2 (Insurance-Company), has supported the award passed by the learned Tribunal, by arguing that the liability has rightly been fastened upon respondents No.1 and 2, as, the vehicle in question was being plied in violation of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.

28. Mr. G.R. Palsra, learned counsel appearing for petitioner has argued that the compensation,
which has been awarded by the learned Tribunal, is on the lower side and the same does not fall within the definition of just compensation.
In addition to this, Mr. Palsra has also argued that it has been proved, in this case, that the deceased was travelling in the vehicle as a care taker of goods.

In such a situation, the .
findings, by virtue of which, the Insurance Company has been exonerated have also been assailed.

29. In order to decide the controversy involved in the of present case, it would be just and appropriate for this Court to discuss the oral, as well as, documentary evidence adduced rt by the parties before the learned Tribunal.

After framing of issues, the petitioner has examined Dr. D.P. Handa, Medical Officer, Zonal Hospital, Mandi, who has conducted the post-mortem examination of the dead body of Sanjay Kumar @ Sanju and proved the copy of the same as Ext.PW-1/A.
31.
Petitioner Jaiwanti herself appeared in the witness box as PW-2 and deposed that on 23.03.2004, her son Sanjay Kumar @ Sanju had expired in the accident, involving offending vehicle.
On the day of accident, her son had gone to Pandoh in order to purchase the articles.
On the evening of the said day, her son had to sell peas crop.
She has given the age of her son as 22 years.
The peas crop was stacked besides the road.
Thereafter, her son was to hire the vehicle.
Thereafter, the crop was to be taken to the market.
During the evening of the said day, one scooterist informed about the accident near Surahi khud.

Her son is stated to be earning .
Rs.5,000-6,000/- per month and during vegetable season, he used to earn Rs.15,000-20,000/- per month.

Lastly, she has deposed that on the next day of the incident, some persons of had delivered,
beddings and quilts, which, her son had purchased for her.
32. In rt cross-examination by learned counsel for respondents No.1 and 2 this witness has deposed that when, the accident had taken place, during those days, peas season was there.
The traders from different parts of the country used to come to purchase the crop.
She has admitted that her son Sanjay and his friend Desh Raj had hired the offending vehicle for transporting the peas crop of different persons, including Brij Lal.
33. In cross-examination by learned counsel for the Insurance-Company, this witness has deposed that her son had gone to Pandoh at about 2.00 p.m.
She has feigned her ignorance about the fact as to from where, her son had purchased the quilts, but, voluntarily stated that the same were purchased for being used in their house.
Her son had not obtained the bills of the same.

As per this witness, the peas crop was yet to be loaded in the offending vehicle and the offending vehicle met with an accident prior to loading the .
crop in it.
She was not present at the time of accident.
34. PW-3 Roop Lal was present on the road during the evening time.
He had noticed that one truck came from of Pandoh side, being driven by its driver in a rash and negligent manner and said vehicle was moving towards Gohar side.

This rt witness has given the signal to stop the vehicle, but,
the driver did not stop it.
After sometime, the vehicle had rolled down from the road due to its fast speed.
Three persons were found there in the injured condition.
One person had died on the spot.
On the spot, some articles were lying scattered.
One bedding, which seemed to be new, was also found lying there.
35. In the cross-examination by the learned counsel for respondents No. 1 and 2, this witness has deposed that his statement was recorded on the next day.
He has admitted that Hem Raj and Sanjay used to sow peas crop.
During that period, when, the accident had taken place, the peas season was on its peak.

He has admitted that some villagers used to sell the crop in the village and some Chunni Lal And Others vs Jaiwanti And Others on 15 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106498979/

He has admitted that at the time of accident, nothing was there in the truck, but, voluntarily stated that prior rt to accident, beddings, rice and flour were loaded in it.
37. By tendering, certified copy of FIR Ext. P-1, statement of Ved Kumar Ext. P-2 and certified copy of statement of Lata Devi Ext.P-3, learned counsel for the petitioner has closed the evidence.

38. To rebut this evidence, respondent No.1 Roshan Lal has appeared in the witness box as RW-1 and deposed that at the relevant time, he has engaged Govind Ram as Cleaner with a direction not to permit any person to travel in the vehicle.
On 23.03.2004, after the accident, his driver has informed him, which according to him, had taken place due to breakage of the tie rod.

He has also deposed that he had been apprised about the fact that when, the offending vehicle, being driven by respondent No.2 reached at Pandoh, the vehicle in question was stopped by respondent No.2 in order to have tea.

In the meanwhile, three persons came there, who had requested respondent No.2 to transport their .

39. RW-2 Govind Ram is the driver of the offending vehicle.
On 23.3.2004, he was on his way back to Darlaghat.

At about 7.00 p.m. when, he reached at Pandoh, then, he had stopped the offending vehicle, in order to have tea, then, Brij Lal, who used to deal in peas crop, came to him and requested him to go to village Chapran, as, he had to purchase the peas crops and the said crop was requested to be transported to Sundernagar vegetable market.
Hem Raj and Sanjay had also requested him, upon which, he has requested Brij Lal to arrange for the labour for loading, upon which, Hem Raj and Sanjay said that they will load the crop in the truck.

sentences.text: RW-4 Mohan Lal was posted as ASI at the relevant time in Police Station, Gohar.
He had investigated the case and FIR in question has been registered, on account of the accident in question.
According to him, it has not come in the investigation that the deceased were carrying any goods with them.
He has not prepared any memo regarding the goods.
41. However, in cross-examination, this witness has deposed that he had not inquired from any-one about the capacity, in which, the deceased were travelling in the offending vehicle.
He has inquired the matter regarding the rash and negligent driving of the driver.
This witness has reached on the spot after one hour from the accident.
The place, where the accident, had taken place is a gorge.

Since, the said place was a gorge, as such, he had not made efforts .
to ascertain the articles which allegedly had fallen out from the vehicle.
According to him, he was concerned for the treatment of the injured.
Pradhan Ved Prakash disclosed to of this witness that the vehicle was hired for loading peas crop from village Chapran.
However, he has feigned ignorance rt that those persons had loaded some articles from Pandoh.
When, this witness has reached on the spot, it was already dark.
During that night, he had not gone to the spot.
He has feigned ignorance about the fact that villagers had delivered the articles found lying there.
He has admitted that Ved Prakash had disclosed to him that one new bedding was found along-with sack of rice and cereals.
42. This is the entire evidence adduced by the parties before the learned Tribunal.

43. In this case, learned Tribunal has awarded a sum of Rs.1,75,000/- along-with interest @ 7.5%
per annum.
However, the liability has been fastened upon respondents No. 1 and 2 by exonerating the Insurance-Company.
The petitioner has not assailed the award.

44. Petitioner Jaiwanti has categorically pleaded in the petition that her son Sanjay @ Sanju had hired the offending vehicle along-with one Hem Raj in order to carry .
various kind of domestic and occupational goods purchased at Pandoh and they were travelling in the truck as care taker of those goods.
of 45.
This stand has been denied by the respondents.
46. The Insurance-Company has not sought any rt permission under Section 170 of the M.V. Act.
The petitioner, in this case, has deposed, in her examination-in-chief that on that day, her son had gone to Pandoh in order to purchase some articles.
On that day, he had to sell the peas crop.
Lastly, she has deposed that on the next day of the incident, her co-villager had handed over new bedding which her son had purchased and was carrying the same in the truck.

sentences.text: The tone and tenor of the cross-examination of respondents No. 1 and 2, as well as respondent No.3 demonstrate that petitioner's version with regard to hiring of offending vehicle has not only been admitted, but, the same has also been probabilised from the cross-examination, as it has been suggested to her that at the time of accident, the season of harvesting of peas crop was in full swing.
She has also admitted that her son and his companion Hem Raj had hired a vehicle for transporting peas crop.

In cross- examination, this witness has deposed that her son had .
purchased the quilt for domestic use.
48. Not only this, PW-3 has also probabilised the stand of the petitioner qua the fact that her son was travelling in the of offending vehicle as owner of the goods.
This witness has categorically stated that on the spot, some articles were rt found scattered along-with one bedding.
49. Roshan Lal, respondent No.1 is the owner of the offending vehicle.
He has deposed on the basis of information given to him by respondent No.2, qua the fact that the offending vehicle was hired by three persons for carrying peas crop from Chapran.
The said crop was to be transported to Sundernagar vegetable market.
Hem Raj and Sanjay had loaded their domestic articles in the vehicle and on the way, the vehicle met with an accident.
RW-2 Govind Ram is the person, who was on the wheels of the offending vehicle, at the relevant time.

He has deposed about the fact that on 23.03.2004, when he was on the way to Darlaghat, when, he had reached at Pandoh and stopped the vehicle in order to have tea, in the meanwhile, Brij Lal, peas trader and two other persons, namely,
Hem Raj and Sanjay came to him.

Brij Lal has requested him to carry the peas crop from Chapran to Sundernagar, upon which, he has requested Brij Lal to arrange .
for the labour.
It is his further case that Hem Raj and Sanjay had agreed to load the peas crop and they have also loaded some domestic articles such as quilt, cereals and rice etc., in of the offending vehicle.
Both of them had agreed to pay the rent and thereafter, they had loaded the articles in the rt offending vehicle and travelled in the same as owner/care taker of those articles.
Brij Lal had proceeded towards Chapran on his scooter.
50. In cross-examination by learned counsel for the Insurance-Company, he has deposed that deceased were travelling in the rear portion of the vehicle along-with their articles.

RW-4, who is the I.O has also deposed that Ved Ram, Pradhan has disclosed him that on the spot one new bedding,
few sacks of rice and cereals were found on the spot.
51. The proceedings under the M.V. Act are summary in nature, where, the liability of the tort-feaser can be fixed, on the principle of preponderance of probability.
Strict Rules of Evidence Act are not applicable to the summary proceedings under the M.V. Act.
Since, the proceedings are summary in nature, as such, pleadings are also not liable to be strictly construed.
If the submissions, as made by learned counsel for the Insurance-Company, are taken to be correct, that .

sentences.text: The bar with regard to of the consideration of evidence beyond pleadings will only be applicable against respondents No. 1 and 2 and not against the petitioner.
rt 52.
While deciding the question, involved in the lis, entire evidence adduced by the parties is to be taken into consideration.
Opportunity of cross-examination has also been given to the Insurance-Company, respondent No.3 to cross-examine RW-1 and RW-2.
It has also not been suggested to them that the evidence given by them is in order to help the petitioner, rather it has been suggested to RW-2 that he is deposing, in order to save his owner.
Despite lengthy cross- examination, nothing material could be elicited from him, from which, an adverse inference could be drawn that these witnesses are deposing in order to help the petitioner.
It has also not been suggested that they are in collusion with the petitioner.

53. From the evidence of PW-3 Roop Lal, which has also been supported by RW-1, RW-2 and RW-4,
the petitioner has probabilised her defence that her son had purchased the .
domestic articles from Pandoh and after loading the same, he was travelling with those articles as owner of the goods.

In such a situation, the learned Tribunal has erroneously of exonerated the Insurance-Company by holding that the Insurance-Company is not liable to pay the compensation,
as rt Sanjay was travelling in the vehicle as a gratuitous passenger.
54.
The term 'gratuitous passenger' has no where been defined in M.V. Act, but, it means one who has taken the lift.

The learned counsel for appearing for the Insurance- Company could not satisfy the judicial conscience of this Court, as, to how the learned Tribunal has held that the deceased was a gratuitous passenger, as, it has been probabilised in this case, that deceased was travelling in the offending vehicle as owner-cum-care taker of the goods.
55. The learned Tribunal, in this case, has exonerated the Insurance-Company and saddled the liability to pay compensation, along-with interest, on the driver and owner of the offending vehicle.
The said findings are not sustainable in the eyes of law, as, considering the low legal literacy rate of Indian masses, it cannot expected from them to purchase the articles against the bills.
The deceased was resident of village Chapran, Tehsil Chachiot, District Mandi, H.P., and generally, .
people of the said area are simpleton in nature and not aware about the fact that the bills/cash memos are required to be obtained.
The hyper technical approach, as, adopted by the of learned Tribunal is not sustainable, keeping in view the fact that normally no-one insists upon the seller to issue cash memos or bills.
rt The evidence of the parties has to be considered as a whole.

sentences.text: It is the specific case of the petitioner, in the claim petition, that Sanjay Kumar and Hem Raj had hired the offending vehicle for loading the goods.

This stand has not only been supported by the driver, but, he has moved a step further by deposing that one Brij Lal had also hired and negotiated him to transport the peas crop from village Chapran to Sundernagar vegetable market.

The peas season was there, at the relevant time, as such, if the evidence of the parties, so adduced is examined on the touch stone of preponderance of probability, then, the case is made out that the deceased was travelling in the offending vehicle as owner-cum-care taker of the goods.
Not only this, he had to load his peas crop and peas crop of Brij Lal, which was to be transported in the offending vehicle.

57. The award is totally silent as to how the deceased .
was a gratuitous passenger, whereas, it is the specific stand of the petitioner that deceased had hired the offending vehicle for transporting his household goods.

This fact has also been of probabilised from the evidence of PW-3 Roop Lal, as well as, RW-4 Mohan Lal, the I.O.
58. rt A Co-ordinate Bench of this Court in a decision dated 22.08.2014 rendered in FAO No. 9 of 2017 a/w FAO No. 226 of 2007 has held that owner of goods cannot be said to be gratuitous passenger.

The relevant Paras 14 to 19 of the judgment are reproduced as under:-
"14.
I have gone through the pleadings and the evidence led by the parties.

It is admitted by all the parties that the deceased has hired the vehicle for transporting his vegetables to Sabzi Mandi and was returning back to his native place in the same vehicle at the time of accident, thus, was owner of the goods, cannot be said to be gratuitous passenger.

15. This Court in a case titled as National Insurance Co. Ltd. versus Kamla and others, reported in 2011 ACJ 1550, has also discussed the same issue while referring to the judgment of the Apex Court in National Insurance Co. Ltd. versus Cholleti Bharatamma, reported in 2008 ACJ 268 (SC) and held that when the passenger had hired the vehicle for transporting his goods for selling and was returning in the same vehicle then the passenger is not unauthorised/gratuitous passenger in the vehicle till he reaches the place from .
where he had hired the vehicle.

rash or negligent driving is not to be proved and, therefore, this decision does not help the appellant.

9. Learned counsel for the appellant had also relied upon the decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Maghi Ram, 2010 ACJ 2096 (HP), wherein a learned Judge of this Court has considered the question and had observed that the Insurance Company is liable in respect of death or bodily injury to any person including the owner of goods or his authorized representative carried in the vehicle.

entities.text: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Maghi Ram, 2010 ACJ 2096 (HP)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was observed that it is apparent that the goods must normally be carried in the vehicle at the time of accident.

10. The allegations made by the petitioners in the petition as well as in the evidence were that the .
deceased had gone after hiring the truck with his vegetable and was coming in the same vehicle when the accident took place.

The learned counsel for the claimants/respondents No. 1 to 4 had relied upon the decision of Hon'ble Punjab &
Haryana High Court in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Urmila, 2008 ACJ 1381 of (P&H), wherein it was observed that a passenger was returning after selling his goods when the vehicle turned turtle due to rash and negligent driving.

entities.text: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Urmila, 2008 ACJ 1381 of (P&H)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Insurance rt Company seeks to avoid its liability on the ground that the deceased was no longer owner of the goods as he had sold them off.
It was observed that the deceased had hired the vehicle for transporting his animals for selling and was returning in the same vehicle.
It was held that the deceased was not an unauthorized/gratuitous passenger in the vehicle till he reached the place from where he had hired the vehicle.

11. The above decision clearly applies to the present facts, which are similar to the facts of the case and accordingly, I am inclined to hold that the deceased was not an unauthorized/ gratuitous passenger.

No conditions of the insurance policy have been proved that the risk of the owner of goods was not covered in the insurance policy and as such, there is no substance in the plea raised by the learned counsel for the appellant, which is rejected accordingly.

16. Applying the test to the instant case, one comes to an inescapable conclusion that the deceased was travelling in the offending vehicle as owner of goods at the time of accident and not as a gratuitous passenger.

17. It was for the insurer to plead and prove that the deceased was a gratuitous passenger, which it has .
failed to do so.

59.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in National Insurance Company vs. Baljeet Kaur and others, 2004(2)
SCC 1, has discussed provisions of Section 147 of M.V. Act as amended by the 1994 Amendment Act.

entities.text:
National Insurance Company vs. Baljeet Kaur and others, 2004(2)
SCC 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paragraphs 17 and 20 of the judgment are reproduced as under:-
"17.
By reason of the 1994 Amendment what was added is "including the owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the vehicle".

The liability of the owner of the vehicle to insure it compulsorily, thus, by reason of the aforementioned amendment included only the owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the vehicle besides the third parties.

The intention of the Parliament,
therefore, could not have been that the words 'any person' occurring in Section 147 would cover all persons who were travelling in a goods carriage in any capacity whatsoever.

If such was the intention there was no necessity of the Parliament to carry out an amendment inasmuch as expression 'any person' contained in sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of sub-section (1) of Section 147 would have included the owner of the goods or his authorised representative .
besides the passengers who are gratuitous or otherwise.

entities.text: sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of sub-section (1) of Section 147
entities.label: PROVISION

sentences.text: 20. It is therefore, manifest that in spite of the amendment of 1994, the effect of the provision contained in Section 147 with respect to persons other than the owner of the goods or his authorized representative remains the same.

Although the owner of the goods or his authorized of representative would now be covered by the policy of insurance in respect of a goods vehicle, it was not the intention of the legislature to provide for the liability of the rt insurer with respect to passengers, especially gratuitous passengers, who were neither contemplated at the time the contract of insurance was entered into, nor any premium was paid to the extent of the benefit of insurance to such category of people."

60. So far as the arguments of learned counsel appearing for respondent No.1/appellants qua the fact that it has not been proved, in this case, that the accident in question had taken place due to rash and negligent driving of respondent No.2 are concerned

, the said arguments do not hold water,
as the factum of accident has been admitted by respondents No. 1 and 2, but, the defence of mechanical defect, which has been taken by them has neither been proved nor probabilised, by leading any cogent evidence.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Mere taking of defence of mechanical defect is not sufficient to hold that there was no negligence on the part of respondent No.2.
Registration of FIR is prima-facie proof of rash and negligent driving against the driver.
Learned counsel for the appellants could not satisfy the judicial conscience of this Court as to how the award, which has been passed by the learned Tribunal, is on of the higher side.
62. No other point has been urged or argued.
63. rt

In view of the discussion made above, the appeal filed by LRs of respondent No. 1 is partly allowed and award passed by the learned Tribunal is modified by directing the Insurance-Company to pay the entire amount of compensation along-with interest, as awarded by the learned Tribunal.
There shall be no order as to costs.
64. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
65. Record be sent down.

Strict Rules of Evidence Act are not applicable to the summary proceedings under the M.V. Act.
